rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes threshold from 'reduction_size <= 32' to 'reduction_size <= 31'. With fixed input shape [16, 256, 256]: dim=0 gives reduction_size=16 (16<=31 TRUE, 16<=32 TRUE, same branch); dim=1 gives reduction_size=256 (256<=31 FALSE, 256<=32 FALSE, same branch); dim=2 gives reduction_size=256 (same as dim=1). The only distinguishing value would be reduction_size=32, which is unreachable with this fixed shape.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation modifies the threshold that determines which kernel (small vs optimized) is selected based on reduction_size. The difference only manifests when reduction_size equals exactly 32: the original would use the small kernel (32 <= 32 is TRUE) while the mutant would use the optimized kernel (32 <= 31 is FALSE). However, the fixed input shape [16, 256, 256] has dimension sizes of 16, 256, and 256. No matter which dimension is chosen for reduction, the reduction_size will be either 16 or 256, never 32. For reduction_size=16, both conditions evaluate to TRUE (same kernel selected). For reduction_size=256, both conditions evaluate to FALSE (same kernel selected). Therefore, the mutation cannot produce any observable difference regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation only affects behavior when reduction_size=32, but the fixed shape [16, 256, 256] provides reduction sizes of 16 or 256, never 32. Killing this mutant would require changing the input shape to have exactly 32 elements along the reduction dimension, which violates the fixed-shape constraint.
rounds.recommendations: When designing mutation tests for kernel dispatch thresholds, ensure the test configuration includes shapes that exercise the exact boundary values. For this kernel, testing with a reduction dimension of size 32 would expose the threshold boundary. Consider adding shape-parameterized tests that hit common power-of-two boundaries (16, 32, 64, etc.) to catch threshold mutations.
